an2.1:2.6: The commentary explains these punishments thus. “Porridge pot”: remove the top of the skull and drop in a hot iron ball so that the brains boil over. “Shell-shave”: grind the skull with gravel until it is smooth. “Rāhu’s mouth”: force open the mouth with a skewer, put in oil and wick, and light it so it burns like the sun swallowed by the titan Rāhu ([sn2.9]() and [sn2.10]()). “Garland of fire”: smear the body with oil and set it alight. “Burning hand”: wrap the hand with oiled rags and set it alight. “Bulrush twist”: flay the skin from the neck down, then twist it into a band by which to hang the victim. “Bark dress”: cut the skin in strips and make it into a garment. “Antelope”: pin the bound victim to the ground and roast them alive. “Meat hook”: flay with double fish-hooks. “Coins”: slice off disks of flesh like coins. “Caustic pickle”: beat the victim, then rub the wounds with caustic solution. “Twisting bar”: pin the victim to the ground by the ears and twirl them by the feet. “Straw mat”: beat them until every bone is broken and the body becomes limp as a mattress.
an2.3:1.1: The Buddha adapts the religious language of _tapas_ (“mortification”, or more literally “fervor, ardor”), applying it to ethical conduct rather than bodily mortification.
an2.5:1.2: “Not being content” (_asantuṭṭhitā_) inverts the usual virtue of contentedness, but the Sutta does not expand, discussing only the second item. The two items are also mentioned, without explanation, at [dn33:1.9.34]() and [an2.177:1.3](); see too [an6.80:1.3]().
an2.6:1.3: The fetters are desire and lust, while the “things that tighten the fetters” (_saṁyojaniya dhamma_) are the pleasures afforded by the senses ([sn35.122]()).
an2.6:2.1: “Boring” here is _nibbidā_. A more literal rendering might be: “dwelling as an observer of disillusionment in respect of things that provoke fetters”.
an2.7:1.3: These three discourses focus on _hiri_ (“conscience”) and _otappa_ (“prudence” or “shame”). These express the inner dimensions of moral life, the sense of right and wrong that guide conduct. | _Hiri_ (Sanskrit _hrī_) is perhaps originally “blushing”, hence bashfulness, modesty, shame, and conscience. It was already a purely psychological factor before the Buddha (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3). The Arthaśāstra notes conscience as a virtue for a lord (6.1.6) but an obstacle to profiteering (9.4.25). | _Ottappa_ (“prudence”) traces either to the root _tap_ in the sense “burn” with regret, perhaps originally “flushed with embarassment”; or _trap_ in the sense “shame, perplexity”. | The commentaries distinguish the two qualities as arising from respectively inner and outer causes, but this does not seem justified by usage. In practice, they are reinforcing synonyms.
an2.9:1.4: [dn26:20.1]() relates a time when this breakdown happens.
an2.9:1.5: For _sambheda_ in the sense of “dissolving, leaking”, see [dn3:1.15.11](), [an5.103:6.4](), [an10.45:4.1](). The commentary to DN 26 says “mixedness, breaking of boundaries”.
an2.10:1.1: The “rains retreat” or “rainy season residence” makes up three of the four months of the rainy season, during which time they may not travel without good reason. Monastics typically enter the rains retreat at the start of the rainy season; the final month is spent in repairing robes and other duties before heading off wandering. If need be, however, they may enter the “second rains” a month later. This is usually if they’re ill, or traveling, or completing unfinished business.
an2.10:1.3: This is explained at [pli-tv-kd3:2.2.6](): “The first should be entered on the day after the full moon of _Asāḷha_, and the second one month after the same full moon.” The month of _Asāḷha_ in the Indian lunar calendar roughly corresponds with the modern July.
an2.10:1.4: This chapter is a good example of the whiplash of abruptly changing topics in the Aṅguttara Nikāya. While the changes appear random, in many cases there are connections that link one discourse to the next. I discuss these structural features in my Introduction to this collection.
